newsitem.title: UK: UK budget not tight enough to ward off rate rises.
newsitem.headline: UK budget not tight enough to ward off rate rises.

text.p: The UK budget on the face of it offered the best of all worlds but the cost of only a neutral package may be interest rate rises further down the road.
The government forecast of rapidly rising consumer spending next year did not sit easily with its target of reducing underlying inflation to 2.5 percent, analysts said.

"It's difficult to see those two as consistent," said John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International. "If the intention of this budget was to avoid rate rises Clarke needed to be far more aggressive."
Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke unveiled a modest one penny cut in the basic rate of income tax, raised his forecast for GDP growth while lowering that for public debt.
He said tax cuts worth two billion pounds had been matched by the same amount of spending cuts.
Clarke also said his budget was aimed at getting underlying inflation, excluding mortgage interest payments, down to 2.5 percent year-on-year.
Meanwhile the Treasury's Red Book, which fleshes out the budget detail, said consumer spending was forecast to grow at 4.25 percent next year.

"That's plausible enough but how do you rein in inflation given that background?" Shepperd asked. He forecast at least one, maybe two interest rate rises, before elections which must be held by May 1997.

Clarke has already raised base rates once recently, on October 30, by a quarter-point to 6.0 percent. Already, there are signs that inflation could be on the up. RPIX underlying inflation jumped to 3.3 percent year-on-year in October.
Martin Weale, research director at the National Institute for Economic Research, and one of Clarke's independent advisers, was even more certain monetary policy must be tightened.

He said next year would not see a 1980s-style boom but the two years after that could see the return of the UK economy's Achilles Heel -- demand running at well above what the economy can supply in the long run.
"It does raise the prospect of another depression so the economy has to be slowed by policy means some time next year and into 1998," Weale said.

The government, as well as tinkering with taxation and spending, said economic growth would reach 3.5 percent next year and the public sector borrowing requirement would fall to 19 billion pounds, from a previous 23.1 billion forecast.
That may look like a golden scenario for a government in the run-up to elections but economists said the tax cuts boosted the part of the economy that least needed it -- the consumer sector.
"He's given far too much to the consumer sector," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at BankAmerica.

"I think the background to the real economy is going to be sufficiently strong that interest rates will have to be hiked again, certainly once, if not twice if the government's unlucky, before the election."
But Shepperd noted an aggressively tight budget to ward off tighter credit was not an option, politically, for Clarke.

David Kern, chief economist at NatWest, said the Chancellor had probably balanced all interests as well as he could. "An ingenious as well as prudent budget...may have delayed and perhaps eased slightly the pressure for higher interest rates."
But he backed the ranks of economists forecasting one and possibly two more quarter-point rate rises before the election.

"In spite of the softness in wholesale prices, the expected acceleration in domestic demand and the higher-than-expected rise in October RPI make it highly probable that the underlying RPI outcome...could be at least 0.5 higher than the Chancellor expects," Kern said.
